name: Venezuela
card_headline: Delcy Rodríguez governs Venezuela under US oversight with no election date, about 320 political prisoners, a $237.5 billion public debt and an earthquake toll above 6,000
card_summary: Delcy Rodríguez has been acting president since US forces captured Nicolás Maduro on 3 January, and she has set no election date. US-backed talks in Caracas have produced a Supreme Court renewal track but no deal on the electoral council. Foro Penal counts about 320 political prisoners. Oil exports run near 1.08 million barrels a day, the government now reports $237.5 billion in public debt, and the June earthquakes killed at least 6,125 people.
card_local: El Pitazo's headline says four rounds of talks have produced no progress toward a presidential election, and Runrun.es reports the government's own debt figure of $237.5 billion. [1][2]
card_international: AP and Reuters report that Rodríguez promised elections at the UN without naming a date, and Reuters reports October oil exports of about 1.08 million barrels a day. [3][4]
card_scholar: WOLA (March) says authoritarian structures remain after Maduro's removal, HRW (May) finds the amnesty law narrow and opaque, and the Atlantic Council (July) describes US bargaining power over a restructuring of about $240 billion. [5][6][7]
context_md: Hugo Chávez took office in 1999 and began consolidating control starting with the judiciary, according to the summary of opposition leader María Corina Machado's 2026 book. [8] More than 2,000 people were arrested after the 2024 presidential election, AP reports. [9] On 3 January 2026 US forces captured Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores, and Vice President Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as interim president on 5 January. [10] Maduro faces drug trafficking charges in the United States and is held in New York. [3] Venezuela's external debt has been in default since 2017. [2] About 7.1 million Venezuelans were displaced abroad by the end of 2025. [11]

sections.title: Rodríguez governs with US backing and has named no election date
sections.body_md:
Delcy Rodríguez has run Venezuela since January. US forces captured Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores on 3 January and she was sworn in as interim president two days later. [10] Carnegie's Jennifer McCoy wrote in January that Washington chose to work with the existing government, putting stability and oil ahead of a democratic transition. [12] The two countries restored diplomatic ties on 5 March, and Donald Trump called Rodríguez "president-elect" on 8 March although she has not been elected, WOLA reports. [5] AP reported in June that unity inside the ruling party is cracking as she shifts Chávez-era policies. [13]

She has not set a date for a vote. At the UN General Assembly in September she said elections would be held and gave no timing. [3] On 29 October she said the political horizon is measured by objectives, not a calendar date. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said elections could ideally be held in 2027 without a guarantee, and the State Department says that under the roadmap she should leave the presidency vacant in 2027. Trump suggested in late October that Venezuela become the "51st state" and elect a governor, an idea Rodríguez has rejected before. [14][15]

María Corina Machado returned on 25 October after more than ten months in exile, following nationwide protests on 22 October that demanded free elections. Rubio said conditions for her safe return were the result of the US-backed talks. The Al Jazeera and AP report carries no government reaction. [16] Rodríguez had called the arrival a show, and Machado rejects a sequence in which regional elections come before the presidential vote. [15]

lenses.local: El Pitazo's headline says four rounds of talks have produced no progress toward presidential elections. [1]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters report that critics say Washington has put free-election demands behind oil and investment deals. [3]
lenses.scholar: WOLA's Laura Cristina Dib wrote in March that the country could consolidate a new form of authoritarianism, and Crisis Group has published an analysis titled "Venezuela after Maduro: Transaction or Transition?" that was not read for this draft. [5][17]

sections.title: The roadmap: a new court first, the electoral council next, no date
sections.body_md:
The negotiations are US-backed and take place behind closed doors at the Gran Meliá hotel in Caracas. Jorge Rodríguez, president of the National Assembly, leads the government team with Jorge Arreaza. Dinorah Figuera leads an opposition delegation that includes Juan Miguel Matheus and Sergio Vergara and represents the National Assembly elected in 2015. [14]

The fourth round opened on 13 November. Earlier rounds began in August and ran through September and October. They agreed a process to renew the Supreme Court and efforts to recover Venezuelan gold held abroad. No deal has been announced on renewing the National Electoral Council, which the US-backed roadmap places first, and no election date is set. [14] Around 18 November eleven human rights organisations, among them Provea, WOLA and CEJIL, asked the National Assembly and the judicial nominations committee for transparency, merit and independence in choosing Supreme Court magistrates. They acknowledged early progress, including a published scoring scale. [18] Press groups told members of the 2015 Assembly on 3 September that they want press freedom on the agenda. [19]

The details of the talks rest largely on a single report that its publisher says was produced by an automated newsroom. Treat the negotiator names and round dates as unconfirmed until a second outlet reports them. [14]

lenses.local: El Diario reports that Provea, WOLA and CEJIL want an open, merit-based process for the Supreme Court. [18]
lenses.international: MercoPress reports that the roadmap puts court and electoral council renewal before a presidential vote and that Rodríguez backs a reform of the National Assembly. [15]
lenses.scholar: McCoy argued in January that new elections should follow independent judicial and electoral bodies, a process likely to outlast the constitutional six-month limit for replacing an absent president. [12]

sections.title: Political prisoners fell from over 750 to about 320, but the legal machinery is intact
sections.body_md:
Foro Penal counted 322 political prisoners as of 5 October: 140 military and 182 civilians, including 31 foreign nationals and 14 women, with 152 convicted. [20] A 12 November headline from La Patilla gives 321. [21] In March WOLA counted at least 659 releases between 8 January and 8 March and at least 759 people still held for political reasons. [5]

The National Assembly approved an amnesty law on 19 February. It covers offences since 1999 linked to political conflict, including the aftermath of the 2024 election, and excludes people convicted of human rights violations, murder, drug trafficking or corruption. [9] Authorities say more than 8,600 people have benefited, including over 300 who had been imprisoned, but they have published no list. HRW found narrow eligibility, vague exclusions and at least ten cases where judges gave no written denial. [6]

The UN Fact-Finding Mission report of 16 September records fewer prolonged detentions and disappearances after 3 January, but also 64 new torture cases, at least 19 officials linked to serious violations still in key posts, and laws against dissent still in force. [22] Provea counted 336 killings by police and military in 2025 and 170 forced disappearances, up 196 percent on 2024. [23][24] On 18 November the Venezuelan Prisons Observatory said 19 of 36 detained military personnel on hunger strike at Ramo Verde showed physical decline after more than 216 hours without food. [18]

lenses.local: El Diario relays Foro Penal's counts and Provea's 2025 figures, and Provea's own report was seen only in search results. [20][23]
lenses.international: AP and HRW report that the amnesty was signed as an admission of political detentions but applied by courts HRW calls non-independent. [9][6]
lenses.scholar: The UN mission says the changes since January are fragile and reversible because the institutional conditions have not changed. [22]

sections.title: Journalists are out of jail but still prosecuted, and Armando.info is blocked
sections.body_md:
The journalists' union SNTP said on 6 September that six journalists and media workers remain prosecuted months after release, and that dozens are in exile. The National College of Journalists (CNP) said that as of 3 January 42 journalists were prosecuted and nearly 30 were deprived of liberty, that seven are now under precautionary measures, and that it has no information on journalists still jailed. [19] The Caracas branch of the CNP recorded 87 aggressions against the press from January to April, including 18 arbitrary detentions, 15 deportations of foreign correspondents and 4 radio station closures. [25]

Blocking continues online. Espacio Público reported on 22 November that 12 websites and 9 VPN tools were effectively blocked, using a threshold of sustained anomaly rates of 60 percent or more. The named sites include EVTV, Vendata and the investigative outlet Armando.info, which measured 60.8 percent. [26] Armando.info is one of the outlets this page would draw on, and its own reporting was not read for this draft.

lenses.local: SNTP and CNP figures differ by a few cases, and El Diario does not reconcile them. [19]
lenses.scholar: The UN mission found that short-term arrests of journalists continued after January, and TalCual reports a Freedom House finding that Venezuela remains not free online (headline only). [22][27]

sections.title: Oil exports hover near 1.08 million barrels a day while wages sit at 14 cents a month
sections.body_md:
Reuters reports October exports of about 1.08 million barrels a day, down 0.5 percent on September, the lowest since February and up 21 percent on a year earlier. Shipments to the United States were about 449,000 barrels a day, Europe 235,000 and India 242,000. Chevron's exports were about 303,000 barrels a day. Crude output rebounded after Maduro's capture to near pre-sanctions levels and has now stagnated. [4]

Households see little of it. The official rate was 919.82 bolívares per dollar on 24 November, and the minimum wage is 130 bolívares a month, about 14 cents, unchanged. [28] The central bank reported monthly inflation of 8.4 percent in September and 6.2 percent in October, relayed by state-run teleSUR. [29] Steve Hanke's measure, reported by El Diario, puts annual inflation at 238.5 percent on 26 October. These are different measures and are not directly comparable. [30] In March a WOLA analysis cited an economist putting the basic basket at $550 a month against average income of $270. [5] On 18 November Corpoelec workers protested over their year-end bonus, and retirees in the sector said they receive 70 percent of promised bonuses. [18]

The IMF resumed dealings with Venezuela in April, the first financial engagement in over two decades. [7] It later gave $346 million in emergency financing after the earthquakes. [31]

lenses.local: TalCual and El Diario report the wage and exchange-rate squeeze. [28][18]
lenses.international: Reuters carries the export data and its breakdown by buyer and seller. [4]
lenses.scholar: The Atlantic Council notes that the US effectively controls the main sources of oil revenue, which gives Washington bargaining power over the economy. [7]

sections.title: The government now says it owes $237.5 billion, and creditors are lining up
sections.body_md:
In a document called Plan Venezuela Renace, the interim government published its first official estimate of public debt: $237.5 billion, about $202 billion of it external. The commercial portion is $116.5 billion, of which $110.1 billion is eurobonds with accrued interest. PDVSA non-financial debt is $67.3 billion, arbitration awards $26.3 billion, bilateral debt (mainly China and Russia) $23.3 billion and multilateral debt $4.2 billion. The figure equals nearly two and a half years of 2025 output, which Runrun.es puts at $98.1 billion. [2]

The Atlantic Council's Bart Piasecki described the contest in July. Centerview Partners advises Venezuela and a creditor committee includes Fidelity, T. Rowe Price and Morgan Stanley. China is owed about $20 billion, and the 2027 bonds rose from 6.25 cents on the dollar in 2020 to about 40 cents after Maduro's removal. The IMF was excluded from the talks at the time of writing. Piasecki argues a fast deal is not the same as a fair one. [7] Trump and Rodríguez discussed restructuring on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, and critics say Washington has put oil and investment deals ahead of election demands. [3]

lenses.local: Runrun.es, TalCual and El Pitazo all carried the $237.5 billion figure from the government plan. [2]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters report that Trump and Rodríguez discussed restructuring in September. [3]
lenses.scholar: The Atlantic Council says the United States holds the strongest hand, but fragmented debt and China's bargaining position complicate talks. [7]

sections.title: The June earthquakes killed at least 6,125 people, and aid is 39 percent funded
sections.body_md:
Two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck on 24 June, hitting La Guaira and Caracas hardest. On 3 August National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez said 6,125 people were confirmed dead and 61,000 had been treated in hospitals. He said 16.5 percent of the debris had been cleared, and a World Bank report puts physical damage at nearly $20 billion. [32]

Estimates differ by source and date. UNDP's preliminary satellite assessment of 26 June put direct physical damage at $6.7 billion, with a range of $4.7 to $8.7 billion, and 8.6 million people exposed to above-moderate shaking, when the official toll was 920. [33] By 25 July the World Bank estimated about 18,000 people homeless and a physical recovery cost near $50 billion, against an earlier UN preliminary figure of $37 billion. The UN estimated up to 51,000 people may be missing, and Venezuela has released no official count. [31]

The Humanitarian Response Plan asks for $931.3 million, including $298 million for the earthquake, and had received $365.1 million, or 39.2 percent, as of 22 July. [34] The United States pledged $300 million. Civil society groups say state controls on information and hostility toward humanitarian groups could slow recovery. [31]

lenses.local: No Venezuelan outlet's earthquake reporting was read for this draft, and TalCual keeps a dedicated earthquakes tag. [32]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera carry the official toll and the World Bank estimates. [32][31]
lenses.scholar: UNDP and the NRC provide the damage and funding figures. [33][34]

sections.title: The United States is now a security partner, and deportations have resumed
sections.body_md:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met Rodríguez at Miraflores on 18 November. El Diario reports he said Venezuela had gone from the most aggressive regional threat to a partner, and that he signed a military cooperation agreement with Defence Minister Gustavo González López. [18] The Rio Times, writing earlier the same day, said no agreement or readout had been made public. [35] The text of the agreement was not seen.

The relationship began with force. ACLED reported that over 150 US aircraft hit at least seven military facilities on 3 January, killing at least 74 Venezuelan and Cuban soldiers and at least three civilians. It also counted 34 US strikes on suspected drug vessels since September 2025, killing at least 110 people, and said the ELN and FARC dissident factions had limited their response to statements. [10] The UN mission documented ties between state authorities and armed pro-government groups known as colectivos. [22]

About 7.1 million Venezuelans were displaced abroad at the end of 2025, and Venezuelan authorities report 1.2 million returns in recent years. The regional response received about 24 percent of the $370 million required. [11] CNN reported on 3 August that the United States resumed deportations to Venezuela after the earthquakes. [36]

lenses.local: El Diario reports the Hegseth visit and the signed agreement. [18]
lenses.international: AP, Reuters and CNN report the deportation flights and the reaction to the Hegseth visit. [36][35]
lenses.scholar: ACLED and UNHCR supply the casualty and displacement counts. [10][11]

timeline.text: US forces capture Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores.
Delcy Rodríguez is sworn in as interim president.
National Assembly approves an amnesty law, signed by Rodríguez.
The United States and Venezuela restore diplomatic and consular ties.
The IMF resumes dealings with Venezuela.
Two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 strike La Guaira and Caracas.
US-backed talks between the government and the opposition begin.
The official earthquake death toll reaches 6,125.
UN Fact-Finding Mission publishes its report on Venezuela.
Rodríguez briefly meets Trump at the UN and promises elections without a date.
María Corina Machado returns after more than ten months abroad.
The fourth round of government-opposition talks opens in Caracas.
Hegseth meets Rodríguez in Caracas; El Diario reports a military cooperation agreement.
The government publishes a public debt estimate of $237.5 billion.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and Al Jazeera file on Venezuela regularly, and Atlantic Council, WOLA, ACLED and Carnegie have published through the year [3][4][5][7]. Local outlets such as Runrun.es, TalCual, El Pitazo and El Diario publish daily, though blocking limits access to some of them [26].

severity.basis: US strikes killed at least 74 soldiers and three civilians in January, and the UN mission documents armed pro-government groups, but ACLED saw only limited armed resistance afterwards [10][22].
The June earthquakes killed at least 6,125 people, about 7.1 million Venezuelans are displaced abroad, and the response plan is 39.2 percent funded [32][11][34].
Foro Penal counts 322 political prisoners, laws against dissent remain in force, no election date exists and press blocking continues [20][22][26].
Public debt is $237.5 billion, annual inflation is estimated at 238.5 percent and the minimum wage is about 14 cents a month [2][30][28].
Prisoner numbers and monthly inflation are falling and oil exports have recovered, while the earthquake and the lack of an election timetable weigh the other way [20][29][4][3].

parts.basis: The United States captured the president, signed a reported military cooperation agreement and controls main oil revenue channels, and China is owed about $20 billion [10][18][7].
Venezuela exports about 1.08 million barrels a day to the United States, Europe and India, and its roughly $240 billion debt is among the largest sovereign restructurings under discussion [4][7].
ELN and FARC dissidents operate along the Colombian border and about 7.1 million Venezuelans live abroad [10][11].
Venezuelans displaced abroad number about 7.1 million, with 1.2 million returns reported by Venezuelan authorities [11].
A US military operation removed a sitting head of state and the US has struck suspected drug vessels, with at least 110 killed by January [10].

summary: Venezuela matters beyond its borders through oil, a very large debt restructuring, the largest displacement in the hemisphere and the precedent of a foreign military capture of a head of state [4][7][11][10].
gi.up: A breakdown of the US-Rodríguez arrangement, renewed US military action, or a disputed election path that sends more people abroad.
gi.down: A credible election timetable, a completed debt restructuring and stable oil output.

gaps: Local sourcing is uneven: El Pitazo, Efecto Cocuyo and Runrunes pages often failed to open, so El Pitazo's talks headline and the La Patilla and El Diario Hanke headlines were seen only in search results.
Efecto Cocuyo, Tal Cual, Armando.info and VTV reporting was not read in full, and no state outlet other than teleSUR is cited.
Crisis Group, Carnegie and CSIS analyses beyond the pieces cited were not opened; Crisis Group pages failed to load and only a title is cited.
Details of the government-opposition talks rest on one Rio Times report whose publisher says it uses an automated newsroom.
The Hegseth agreement text and El Diario's report that it was signed could not be confirmed against a second source.
Inflation figures conflict by measure: the central bank's monthly rates are relayed by state-run teleSUR, and Hanke's annual estimate is known only from a headline.
The UN Fact-Finding Mission and Provea reports were read through El Diario summaries, not the documents.
Earthquake damage estimates differ ($6.7 billion UNDP, nearly $20 billion World Bank, $37 to $50 billion recovery) and no official missing-person count exists.
Essequibo, the 2024 election dispute and the detailed security picture are not covered in depth.
Podcast and media coverage is thin: one podcast episode and one documentary were verified.
Fact-checks cover two claims only, and both rest on PolitiFact.

factchecks.claim: Nicolás Maduro released prisoners from Venezuelan jails and sent them to the US southern border.
factchecks.evidence: PolitiFact found no academic or government reports of this. Immigration experts and Venezuelan criminologists said there is no known practice of sending prisoners abroad, and the claim traces to a 2022 Breitbart article based on an anonymous source.

sources.title: PolitiFact FL: DeSantis repeats unfounded claim that Maduro sent freed Venezuelan prisoners to the US

factchecks.claim: Maduro's government directed Tren de Aragua and sent its members to the United States.
factchecks.evidence: PolitiFact cites a May 2025 National Intelligence Council memo that found no evidence the Maduro government directed the gang or sent its members to the US. PBS NewsHour also published a fact-check of Trump's claims after the January raid, which was seen by headline only.
